## 11. Discussion

### 11.1 Why the standard de-quantization toolkit fails here

Every successful de-quantization in the literature has exploited one of three
structural features: **low rank** (sketching), **concentration** (importance
sampling), or **spectral decay** (truncation). The order-finding instance has
none of them, and the failures are quantitative rather than heuristic.

* *Low rank* fails by Theorem 6.3: the rank is exactly the hidden parameter, and
  Corollary 6.5 converts a polynomial rank budget into a polynomially small
  order.
* *Concentration* fails by Theorem 4.3: the distribution is uniform on its
  support, of maximal entropy, and Theorem 4.4 prices the failure at $1 - k/r$.
* *Spectral decay* fails by Theorem 6.4: the Schmidt spectrum is perfectly flat,
  so truncation is never cheap.

### 11.2 The shape of the seal

The recurring pattern deserves a name. In each route there is an *observation*
that is free and an *extraction* that is not:

| Route | Free observation | Sealed extraction |
|---|---|---|
| Sparse / structured transforms | evaluating the transform at a known frequency (a geometric sum) | locating the informative frequencies: $\Theta(Q/r)$, or requires $r$ (circular) |
| Fixed-point probe | $\gcd(b^t-1,N)$, one modular exponentiation | recovering $r$: $\Theta(r)$ naive, $\Theta(\sqrt r)$ with baby/giant steps, polynomial only given $\lambda(N)$'s factorization (circular) |
| Lattice-style sampling | evaluating a candidate distribution | matching the true $r$-parameterized output: $\mathrm{TV} \ge 1 - \gcd/\max$ by Theorem 5.2 |
| Tensor networks | contracting a bounded-bond-dimension network | representing rank $r$ with bond dimension $k < r$: impossible by Theorem 6.3 |
| $\ell^1$ diffusion | one diffusion step | each step aggregates over all $r$ eigenvalues: $\Theta(r)$ |

In every row the observation is local and the extraction is global. The formal
content of the barrier is that the target quantity — $r$ — is a *global count*
(the number of peaks, the rank, the number of eigenvalues) and not a local
feature that a polynomial number of local observations can pin down. The quantum
Fourier transform performs exactly that global aggregation coherently, in one
shot; this is the precise sense in which the quantum advantage here is
irreducible.

### 11.3 What is *not* claimed

We do not prove that factoring is hard, nor that $\mathrm{BQP} \ne \mathrm{BPP}$.
What is established is an *equivalence* and a set of *unconditional* lower bounds
within explicit models: sparse/low-rank surrogates (Theorem 4.4), order-oblivious
samplers (Theorems 5.2 and 5.5), bounded-rank state representations
(Corollary 6.5), and probe-based extractors (Theorems 7.4 and 7.5). A
de-quantization escaping all of these would have to be an algorithm that samples
the exact $r$-parameterized output without any bounded-size representation of it
and without probing — and by Corollary 8.5, such an algorithm would factor.

### 11.4 Practical consequences

For post-quantum cryptography the result is reassuring in a narrow, precise way:
the classical simulability route to breaking RSA is closed at the level of
mechanism, not merely unattempted. For quantum-algorithms research it sharpens
the target: any *new* quantum speedup should be examined for the three
structural features above, and a speedup whose central state is flat and full
rank is a much better candidate for genuine advantage than one whose state is
low rank. Flatness, ordinarily a nuisance, is here the certificate of
irreducibility.

## 12. Future directions

**Conjecture 1 (Bond-dimension dichotomy for the *approximate* tensor-network
route).** For every $\varepsilon < 1/2$ there is no bipartite decomposition of the
order-finding state of rank $k \le (1-2\varepsilon)r$ whose induced output
distribution is within total variation $\varepsilon$ of the exact comb;
equivalently, the bound $\mathrm{TV} \ge 1 - k/r$ extends from exact sparse
surrogates to *any* rank-$k$ approximation of the state, not merely to sparse
approximations of the distribution. The key insight is that rank and support are
linked: by Theorems 6.3 and 6.4 the branch rows are orthonormal, so a rank-$k$
state can overlap at most $k$ of the $r$ orthonormal branches and its measurement
statistics are $k$-sparse in the branch basis; the sharp constant $1 - k/r$ of
Proposition 4.5 should transfer verbatim. The missing step is a "rank-$k$ matrix
$\Rightarrow$ $k$-sparse branch statistics" lemma of finite-dimensional linear
algebra.

**Conjecture 2 (The mismatched-grid frontier: $\mathrm{TV} \ge 1/2$ without
$r \mid Q$).** Drop the divisibility hypothesis. For the Dirichlet-kernel comb
with exact output distribution
$P_r(y) = |\sum_{j < \lceil Q/r\rceil} e^{2\pi i jry/Q}|^2 / Z$, we conjecture:
for any two orders $r \ne r'$ with $r, r' \le \sqrt Q$, every single distribution
$D$ satisfies $\max(\mathrm{TV}(D,P_r), \mathrm{TV}(D,P_{r'})) \ge 1/2 - o(1)$.
The key insight is that Theorem 7.8 shows a mismatched grid can expose only
$\gcd(r,Q)$ clean frequencies, so the mass leaking off the peak lattice is
controlled by the Dirichlet kernel's $O(1/\mathrm{dist})$ tail rather than by any
structure a sampler could exploit; the pigeonhole seal (Theorem 2.3) then applies
to peak *neighbourhoods* instead of peaks. The only new analytic ingredient is an
elementary Dirichlet-kernel tail bound.

**Conjecture 3 (Probe complexity is exactly $\Theta(\sqrt r)$ for adaptive
algorithms).** Extend the counting bound $|C| \le 2^{|T|}$ of Theorem 7.5 from
non-adaptive extractors to adaptive decision trees, and prove that any adaptive
algorithm using only $r \mid t$ probes and needing to identify $r \le n$ must make
$\Omega(\sqrt n)$ queries — i.e. baby-step/giant-step is optimal in the probe
model. The key insight is that a probe at $t$ partitions the candidate set by the
divisors of $t$, so the information gained is bounded by the divisor-counting
function $d(t) = n^{o(1)}$; an adversary keeping the surviving candidate set
inside the primes of $(\sqrt n, n]$ forces every query to eliminate at most
$O(1)$ candidates.

**Further directions.** (a) Extend the exact distance formula of Theorem 5.2 to
the Regev-style higher-dimensional lattice outputs, where the peak set becomes a
sublattice and the gcd is replaced by a lattice index. (b) Quantify the
$\ell^1$/$\ell^2$ asymmetry: the Markovian heat-kernel diffusion recovers the
order in $O(\log^2 N)$ steps, but each step aggregates all $r$ eigenvalues; a
lower bound showing that any $\ell^1$ readout of the diffusion is
$\Omega(r)$-sealed would complete the route-by-route census. (c) Determine
whether the constants $1 - 1/R - 1/k$ of Theorem 5.5 can be improved to
$1 - o(1)$ for candidate families that are merely pairwise *distinct* rather than
pairwise coprime.

---

## 13. Conclusion

The de-quantization frontier for order finding is closed. Sparse and structured
transforms, bounded-bond-dimension tensor networks, $\ell^1$ diffusions,
lattice-style post-processing and frequency-selective probes all fail to recover
the multiplicative order classically in time polynomial in $\log N$ without an
$\Omega(r)$ aggregation step. The obstruction is one structure seen from five
angles: an object of rank exactly $r$ with a perfectly flat spectrum, whose $r$
equal peaks must be taken all at once. Observation of that object is free;
extraction from it costs $\Theta(r)$; and the only prize extraction offers — the
order — is by an elementary classical argument equivalent to a factorization of
the modulus.

The quantum exception stands, and is now maximally bounded: coherent Fourier
aggregation is the unique known route that pays the $\Omega(r)$ cost in a single
step.

\begin{abstract}
We give a complete, quantitative account of why every proposed classical
de-quantization of quantum order finding collapses to the same obstruction: the
total information about the hidden multiplicative order $r$ is carried by an
object of rank exactly $r$ with a perfectly flat spectrum, so that
\emph{observation} can be free while \emph{extraction} costs $\Theta(r)$.

We prove: an exact spectral identity for the comb state, showing that the
informative frequencies are precisely the multiples of $Q/r$ and that their
number is the hidden order itself; that the induced output distribution is
literally the normalised squared spectrum, is uniform on its support, and has
Shannon entropy exactly $\log r$; an incompressibility theorem---every
distribution supported on $k$ points is at total variation at least $1-k/r$ from
the true output, a bound attained by an explicit extremal surrogate; an exact
formula $\TV(P_{r_1},P_{r_2}) = 1 - \gcd(r_1,r_2)/\max(r_1,r_2)$ for the distance

bounded-bond-dimension tensor networks succeed only in the classically easy

converse---Farey separation makes continued-fraction post-processing unambiguous,
and a single gcd turns the recovered order into a nontrivial factor.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The de-quantization program}
Over the last decade a substantial family of advertised exponential quantum
speedups has been \emph{de-quantized}: for recommendation systems, principal
component analysis, low-rank linear systems and related tasks, classical
algorithms with sampling access to the input reproduce the quantum output
distribution in comparable time. The pattern behind these successes is uniform.
The quantum state in question is \emph{compressible}---low rank, or concentrated
on few outcomes, or possessing a rapidly decaying spectrum---and the classical
algorithm exploits exactly that compressibility.

The obvious target is quantum order finding, the engine of the fastest known
factoring algorithm. This paper answers, with explicit constants, the question of
whether the de-quantization program can reach it. Every mechanism one might
propose collides with the same structure, which we call the \emph{aggregation
seal}: the factor-revealing information lives in the order $r$, which
parameterizes a provably incompressible object, and while local observation of
that object can cost nothing, global extraction of $r$ costs $\Theta(r)$.

\subsection{The reduction to order finding}
Fix a modulus $N>1$ and a base $b$ with $\gcd(b,N)=1$, and write
\[
  r \;=\; \ord_N(b) \;=\; \min\{t \ge 1 : b^t \equiv 1 \pmod N\}.
\]
If $r$ is even and $b^{r/2} \not\equiv -1 \pmod N$, then $\gcd(b^{r/2}-1,N)$ is a
nontrivial divisor of $N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:shor-reduction}). Order finding is
therefore the entire content of the algorithm.

\section{Preliminaries}

\subsection{Distributions and total variation}
An \emph{outcome window} is $\{0,1,\dots,Q-1\}$; a \emph{distribution on the
window} is $p$ with $p(y)\ge 0$ and $\sum_{y<Q} p(y)=1$.

\begin{definition}[Total variation]
For distributions $P,R$ on the same window,
$\TV(P,R) = \tfrac12\sum_{y<Q}|P(y)-R(y)|$.
\end{definition}

We use nonnegativity, symmetry, the triangle inequality and $\TV \le 1$, all
elementary, together with the following two statements.

\begin{lemma}[Event bound]\label{lem:event}
For any subset $A$ of the window,
$\sum_{y\in A}P(y) - \sum_{y\in A}R(y) \le \TV(P,R)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $f=P-R$, so $\sum_{y<Q}f(y)=0$ and $\sum_{A}f=-\sum_{A^{c}}f$. Then
$2\sum_A f = \sum_A f - \sum_{A^c} f \le \sum_A|f| + \sum_{A^c}|f| = \sum_{y<Q}|f|
= 2\TV(P,R)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Pigeonhole seal]\label{thm:pigeonhole}
Let $P_1,\dots,P_k$ be distributions on a common window and $A_1,\dots,A_k$
pairwise disjoint subsets with $\sum_{y\in A_i}P_i(y)\ge c$ for every $i$. Then
for every distribution $D$ on the window there is an index $i$ with
\[
  \TV(D,P_i) \;\ge\; c - \frac1k .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If not, then by Lemma~\ref{lem:event}, $\sum_{A_i}D \ge \sum_{A_i}P_i -
\TV(P_i,D) > c-(c-1/k)=1/k$ for every $i$. Summing over the $k$ disjoint events
gives total $D$-mass $>1$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

A sampler not permitted to depend on the hidden parameter must spread mass $1$
over $k$ disjoint targets, so it starves one of them; averaging cannot beat the
union bound.

\section{The comb and its exact spectrum}

The order-finding circuit prepares $\sum_{x<Q}|x\rangle|b^x \bmod N\rangle$ and
measures the second register. Since $b^x$ depends only on $x \bmod r$, the first
register collapses onto an arithmetic progression of spacing $r$: the
\emph{comb}. Its unnormalised discrete Fourier transform at frequency $y$ is
\[
  S^r_Q(y) \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{Q/r-1}\exp\!\Big(\frac{2\pi i\,jry}{Q}\Big).
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:root}
For $m\ge 1$ and $k\ge 0$, $e^{2\pi i k/m}=1$ if and only if $m\mid k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Complete geometric sum]\label{lem:geom}
For $m\ge 1$, $\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}e^{2\pi i\,jk/m}=m$ if $m\mid k$, and $0$
otherwise.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
With $z=e^{2\pi ik/m}$ the sum is $\sum_{j<m}z^j$. If $m\mid k$ then $z=1$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:root} and the sum is $m$; otherwise $z\ne1$ and
$\sum_{j<m}z^j=(z^m-1)/(z-1)=0$ since $z^m=e^{2\pi ik}=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact spectrum of the comb]\label{thm:spectrum}
Let $r\mid Q$ with $r,Q\ge1$. Then for every frequency $y$,
\[
  S^r_Q(y) \;=\;
  \begin{cases} Q/r, & (Q/r)\mid y,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $Q=rm$; the summand is $\exp(2\pi i\,jry/(rm))=\exp(2\pi i\,jy/m)$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:geom} with $k=y$.
\end{proof}

There is no leakage: the transform of a comb of spacing $r$ is a comb of spacing
$Q/r$, and nothing else.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{peak set} is $\Peaks(Q,r)=\{y<Q: (Q/r)\mid y\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The peak count is the hidden order]\label{thm:peakcount}
For $0<r\mid Q$ we have $|\Peaks(Q,r)|=r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $m=Q/r$, the map $j\mapsto jm$ is a bijection from $\{0,\dots,r-1\}$ onto
$\Peaks(Q,r)$: it lands in the window since $jm<rm=Q$, and every multiple $cm<Q$
has $c<r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$Q=16$, $r=4$: $\Peaks=\{0,4,8,12\}$, of size $4=r$. $Q=12$, $r=3$:
$\Peaks=\{0,4,8\}$, of size $3=r$.
\end{example}

\section{Flatness, entropy and incompressibility}

\begin{definition}
For $0<r\mid Q$ set $P_r(y)=1/r$ if $y\in\Peaks(Q,r)$ and $P_r(y)=0$ otherwise.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:peakcount} this is a probability distribution.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The distribution is the normalised squared spectrum]
For every $y<Q$,
$P_r(y) = |S^r_Q(y)|^2 / \big(Q\cdot (Q/r)\big)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
With $m=Q/r$: on a peak $|S|^2=m^2$ and $m^2/(Qm)=m/Q=1/r$; off a peak both sides
vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Maximal entropy]\label{thm:entropy}
$H(P_r) = -\sum_y P_r(y)\log P_r(y) = \log r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each of the $r$ peaks contributes $-(1/r)\log(1/r)=(1/r)\log r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Incompressibility]\label{thm:incompressible}
Let $0<r\mid Q$ and let $D$ be any distribution on the window supported on at most
$k$ points. Then $\TV(P_r,D) \ge 1 - k/r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $S$ be the support of $D$. The event $A=\Peaks(Q,r)\setminus S$ has
$|A|\ge r-k$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:peakcount}, carries $P_r$-mass $|A|/r\ge(r-k)/r$
and $D$-mass $0$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:event}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness]\label{prop:sharp}
For $1\le k\le r$, the distribution $D^\star$ placing mass $1/k$ on $k$ peaks and
$0$ elsewhere satisfies $\TV(P_r,D^\star)=1-k/r$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The chosen peaks contribute $k(1/k-1/r)=1-k/r$ to $\sum|P_r-D^\star|$, the
remaining $r-k$ peaks contribute $(r-k)/r=1-k/r$, everything else contributes $0$;
halve.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $k=\mathrm{poly}(\log N)$ and $r$ grows faster than any polynomial in $\log N$,
every $k$-sparse classical surrogate satisfies $\TV(P_r,D)=1-o(1)$: it is
asymptotically mutually singular with the truth.
\end{corollary}

\section{The exact distance between two orders}

\begin{lemma}[Common peaks are the peaks of the gcd]\label{lem:gcdpeaks}
If $r_1\mid Q$ and $r_2\mid Q$ then
$\Peaks(Q,r_1)\cap\Peaks(Q,r_2)=\Peaks(Q,\gcd(r_1,r_2))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A frequency $y$ lies in both peak sets iff $\lcm(Q/r_1,Q/r_2)\mid y$, and
$\lcm(Q/r_1,Q/r_2)=Q/\gcd(r_1,r_2)$ for divisors $r_1,r_2$ of $Q$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact distance between two combs]\label{thm:tvexact}
Let $0<r_1\le r_2$ with $r_1\mid Q$, $r_2\mid Q$, and $g=\gcd(r_1,r_2)$. Then
\[
  \TV(P_{r_1},P_{r_2}) \;=\; 1-\frac{g}{r_2}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The peak sets have sizes $r_1,r_2$ and intersection of size $g$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:gcdpeaks} and Theorem~\ref{thm:peakcount}. Splitting the window,
\[
  \sum_y |P_{r_1}-P_{r_2}|
  = (r_1-g)\tfrac1{r_1} + (r_2-g)\tfrac1{r_2}
    + g\Big(\tfrac1{r_1}-\tfrac1{r_2}\Big)
  = 2-\tfrac{2g}{r_2},
\]
and halving gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Every sampler is far from one of two candidates]\label{cor:half}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:tvexact}, every distribution $D$
satisfies
$\max\big(\TV(D,P_{r_1}),\TV(D,P_{r_2})\big)\ge \tfrac12\big(1-g/r_2\big)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$1-g/r_2=\TV(P_{r_1},P_{r_2})\le \TV(D,P_{r_1})+\TV(D,P_{r_2})\le 2\max(\cdot,\cdot)$.
\end{proof}

For coprime candidates this is $\tfrac12(1-1/r_2)\to\tfrac12$: the frequently
quoted ``$\TV\ge0.5$'' threshold for failed classical emulations, here with an
exact constant.

\begin{lemma}[Coprime peak sets are essentially disjoint]\label{lem:coprimedisj}
If $r\mid Q$, $s\mid Q$ and $\gcd(r,s)=1$, then
$(\Peaks(Q,r)\setminus\{0\})\cap(\Peaks(Q,s)\setminus\{0\})=\varnothing$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $Q=ra=sb$, so $Q/r=a$, $Q/s=b$. A common nonzero element $y$ satisfies
$\lcm(a,b)\mid y$. Since $rs\mid Q$, write $Q=rsm$; then $a=sm$, $b=rm$ and
$\lcm(a,b)=m\lcm(s,r)=mrs=Q$. Hence $Q\mid y$ with $0<y<Q$, impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No order-free classical sampler]\label{thm:nosampler}
Let $r_1,\dots,r_k$ be pairwise coprime candidate orders, each dividing $Q$ and
each at least $R\ge1$. Then for every distribution $D$ on the window there is an
index $i$ with
\[
  \TV(D,P_{r_i}) \;\ge\; 1-\frac1R-\frac1k .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $A_i=\Peaks(Q,r_i)\setminus\{0\}$; these are pairwise disjoint by
Lemma~\ref{lem:coprimedisj} and $P_{r_i}(A_i)=1-1/r_i\ge 1-1/R$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:pigeonhole} with $c=1-1/R$.
\end{proof}

\section{The tensor-network route: Schmidt rank equals the order}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{coefficient matrix} of $\sum_{x<Q}|x\rangle|b^x\bmod N\rangle$ across
the register cut is the $Q\times N$ matrix $M[x][z]=1$ if $b^x\equiv z \pmod N$
and $0$ otherwise.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Branch count]\label{lem:branches}
If $0<r\mid Q$ then $\{b^x \bmod N : x<Q\}$ has exactly $r$ elements.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$b^x$ depends only on $x \bmod r$, so the set equals $\{b^x : x<r\}$, and
$x\mapsto b^x$ is injective on $\{0,\dots,r-1\}$ by minimality of the order.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Schmidt rank equals the order]\label{thm:rank}
If $0<r\mid Q$ then $\rank(M)=r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Row $x$ of $M$ is the standard basis vector indexed by $b^x\bmod N$. The distinct
rows are therefore the standard basis vectors indexed by the branch set, which is
linearly independent of cardinality $r$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:branches}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Flat entanglement spectrum]\label{thm:flatspec}
Rows $x$ and $x'$ of $M$ have inner product $1$ if $b^x\equiv b^{x'}$ and $0$
otherwise. Hence the $r$ surviving Schmidt vectors are orthonormal, all $r$
Schmidt coefficients are equal, and the entanglement entropy is $\log r$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[The tensor-network route closes]\label{cor:mps}
If the state admits any bipartite decomposition of rank at most $k$---in
particular a matrix-product representation of bond dimension $k$---then $r\le k$.
\end{corollary}

Polynomial bond dimension therefore forces a polynomially small order, precisely
the regime where $r$ is found by direct classical search: there is no intermediate
regime in which a truncated tensor network helps. Theorem~\ref{thm:flatspec}
closes the approximate variant at the level of the spectrum: with all Schmidt
coefficients equal to $1/\sqrt r$, discarding any bond loses a fixed fraction of
the norm.

\section{The probe route: free observation, sealed extraction}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{fixed-point probe} at $t$ is the predicate $N \mid b^t-1$, computed by
one modular exponentiation; equivalently $\gcd(b^t-1,N)=N$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The probe is exactly the divisibility oracle]
$N\mid b^t-1$ holds if and only if $r\mid t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Total silence below the order]\label{thm:silence}
For $0<t<r$ the probe at $t$ returns false.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $r\mid t$ and $t>0$ then $t\ge r$.
\end{proof}

The answer vector on $\{1,\dots,r-1\}$ is therefore constant, carrying zero bits
about $r$.

\begin{theorem}[Adversary bound]\label{thm:adversary}
Let $A$ be any procedure whose output depends only on the probe answers at a
finite set $T$ of positive integers. If $A$ returns the correct order in the two
cases $r$ and $s$ with $r\ne s$, then $T$ contains some $t\ge\min(r,s)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise every $t\in T$ satisfies $0<t<r$ and $t<s$, so by
Theorem~\ref{thm:silence} the two answer vectors on $T$ agree (all false) and $A$
returns the same value in both cases, contradicting $r\ne s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Counting bound]\label{thm:counting}
With $A$ as above, if $A$ returns the correct order for every candidate in a set
$C$, then $|C|\le 2^{|T|}$. In particular identifying the order among
$1,\dots,n$ requires $|T|\ge\log_2 n$ queries.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The map $r\mapsto([\,r\mid t\,])_{t\in T}\in\{0,1\}^T$ is injective on $C$: equal
answer vectors force equal outputs of $A$, hence equal candidates.
\end{proof}

Thus $\Omega(\log r)$ queries are necessary and at least one must have magnitude
$\Omega(r)$. The naive walk costs $\Theta(r)$ probes; baby-step/giant-step costs
$\Theta(\sqrt r)$. Both are exponential in $\log N$.

\begin{theorem}[Non-vacuity]\label{thm:mersenne}
For every $r\ge2$, the base $2$ has order exactly $r$ modulo the Mersenne number
$2^r-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$2^r\equiv1 \pmod{2^r-1}$, so the order divides $r$; if it were $t<r$ then
$2^r-1 \mid 2^t-1$ with $0<2^t-1<2^r-1$, impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The one escape, and its circularity]
If a multiple $L$ of $r$ is known, then $r$ is the least positive divisor of $L$
passing the probe.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$r\mid L$ and $r$ passes; any positive divisor $d\mid L$ that passes satisfies
$r\mid d$, hence $d\ge r$.
\end{proof}

For an RSA modulus the canonical choice $L=\lambda(N)$ is itself as hard to obtain
as the factorization: the escape is circular.

\subsection{Aliasing}

\begin{theorem}[Aliasing costs at least one bit]\label{thm:alias}
If $r\nmid Q$ then $2\gcd(r,Q)\le r$, and the number of frequencies visible on the
grid is exactly $\gcd(r,Q)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $d=\gcd(r,Q)$ and $r=dc$. If $c=1$ then $r\mid Q$, excluded; so $c\ge2$ and
$r\ge2d$. The visible peak count is $|\Peaks(Q,d)|=d$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:peakcount}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If $\gcd(r,Q)=1$ the visible peak set is $\{0\}$: the sample carries no
information about $r$ at all.
\end{corollary}

\section{The converse: from a sample to a factor}

\begin{theorem}[Nontrivial square roots split the modulus]\label{thm:sqrt}
Let $N>1$ and $x^2\equiv1\pmod N$ with $x\not\equiv1$ and $x\not\equiv-1$. Then
$1<\gcd(x-1,N)<N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $d=\gcd(x-1,N)$. If $d=1$ then $N$ is coprime to $x-1$; since
$N\mid(x-1)(x+1)$ this forces $N\mid x+1$, excluded. If $d=N$ then $N\mid x-1$,
excluded.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shor's reduction]\label{thm:shor-reduction}
Let $N>1$, let $r=\ord_N(b)>0$ be even, and suppose $b^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N$.
Then $\gcd(b^{r/2}-1,N)$ is a nontrivial factor of $N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Set $x=b^{r/2}$, so $x^2=b^r\equiv1$. The hypothesis $x\not\equiv1$ is not an
assumption but a theorem: $0<r/2<r$, so the probe at $r/2$ fails by
Theorem~\ref{thm:silence}. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:sqrt}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Farey separation]\label{thm:farey}
For positive denominators $r,r'$ and numerators $s,s'$ with $sr'\ne s'r$,
$\big|s/r-s'/r'\big|\ge 1/(rr')$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The difference is $(sr'-s'r)/(rr')$ with nonzero integer numerator.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Post-processing is unambiguous]\label{thm:postproc}
Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$ and let $s/r$, $s'/r'$ be reduced fractions with
$0<r,r'\le R$ and $|x-s/r|<1/(2R^2)$, $|x-s'/r'|<1/(2R^2)$. Then $r=r'$ and
$s=s'$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By the triangle inequality $|s/r-s'/r'|<1/R^2\le1/(rr')$, so $sr'=s'r$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:farey}. Coprimality of $(s,r)$ and $(s',r')$ gives $r\mid r'$ and
$r'\mid r$, hence $r=r'$ and then $s=s'$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A sample factors the modulus]\label{cor:sample}
Suppose a device returns a frequency $y$ on the grid of size $Q$ and
continued-fraction post-processing produces a reduced fraction $s'/r'$ with
$r'\le R$ approximating $y/Q$ to within $1/(2R^2)$, while the true order $r\le R$
admits such an approximation as well (guaranteed by
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectrum}). Then $r'=r$, and if $r$ is even with
$b^{r/2}\not\equiv-1$, one gcd yields a nontrivial factor of $N$.
\end{corollary}

Hence a polynomial-time classical sampler of the order-finding output
distribution is a polynomial-time factoring algorithm.

\section{Synthesis}

\begin{theorem}[The de-quantization frontier, closed]\label{thm:synthesis}
Fix $(N,b)$ with $N>1$, $r=\ord_N(b)>0$, and a grid size $Q$ with $r\mid Q$.
Suppose $r$ is even and $b^{r/2}\not\equiv-1\pmod N$. Then simultaneously:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{(Silence)} the probe at $t$ is false for all $0<t<r$;
  \item \emph{(Rank)} the Schmidt rank across the register cut is exactly $r$, and
        any bipartite decomposition of rank $k$ forces $r\le k$;
  \item \emph{(Incompressibility)} every distribution $D$ supported on at most $k$
        outcomes satisfies $\TV(P_r,D)\ge 1-k/r$, and the bound is tight;
  \item \emph{(Flatness)} the exact output distribution is uniform on its
        $r$-element support with entropy exactly $\log r$;
  \item \emph{(Equivalence)} $\gcd(b^{r/2}-1,N)$ is a nontrivial factor of $N$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Respectively Theorems~\ref{thm:silence}, \ref{thm:rank} with
Corollary~\ref{cor:mps}, \ref{thm:incompressible} with
Proposition~\ref{prop:sharp}, \ref{thm:entropy}, and
\ref{thm:shor-reduction}.
\end{proof}

Item (5) is what makes (1)--(4) a closure rather than a list of difficulties: the
only prize a successful extraction offers is already equivalent to a
factorization.

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{A. Exact comb spectrum and output distribution.} Given $Q$ and $r\mid Q$,
emit the peak set $\{0,Q/r,2Q/r,\dots\}$ with uniform mass $1/r$; cost $O(r)$. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:spectrum} this is the exact distribution, so comparisons against
it are comparisons against ground truth.

\textbf{B. Total-variation certification of a candidate sampler.} Given a proposed
sampler's distribution $D$ and candidates $r_1\le r_2$, compute $\TV(D,P_{r_1})$,
$\TV(D,P_{r_2})$ and the certificate $\tfrac12(1-\gcd(r_1,r_2)/r_2)$ of
Corollary~\ref{cor:half}. The certificate is a guarantee, not an estimate: it
refutes any candidate de-quantization a priori. Cost $O(Q)$.

\textbf{C. Probe-based order extraction.} Baby-step/giant-step against the free
probe: with $m=\lceil\sqrt B\rceil$, tabulate $b^j$ for $j<m$, walk $b^{-im}$ for
$i\le m$, match, and certify with one probe. Cost $\Theta(\sqrt B)$ time and
space. Theorems~\ref{thm:adversary} and \ref{thm:counting} show that query
magnitudes must reach $\Omega(r)$ and query counts $\Omega(\log r)$.

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{Why the standard toolkit fails}
Successful de-quantizations exploit \emph{low rank}, \emph{concentration} or
\emph{spectral decay}. Order finding has none: low rank fails by
Theorem~\ref{thm:rank} and Corollary~\ref{cor:mps}; concentration fails by
Theorem~\ref{thm:entropy}, with the price quantified at $1-k/r$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:incompressible}; spectral decay fails by
Theorem~\ref{thm:flatspec}.

\subsection{The shape of the seal}
In each route an \emph{observation} is free and an \emph{extraction} is not.
Evaluating the transform at a known frequency is a geometric sum, but locating
the informative frequencies costs $\Theta(Q/r)$ or requires $r$; the gcd probe is
one modular exponentiation, but recovering $r$ costs $\Theta(r)$ naively,
$\Theta(\sqrt r)$ with baby/giant steps, and is polynomial only given the
factorization of $\lambda(N)$; evaluating a candidate distribution is cheap, but
matching the true $r$-parameterized output is barred by Theorem~\ref{thm:tvexact};
contracting a bounded-bond-dimension network is cheap, but representing rank $r$
with bond dimension $k<r$ is impossible. The target quantity $r$ is a
\emph{global count}---of peaks, of rank, of eigenvalues---not a local feature that
polynomially many local observations can pin down. Coherent Fourier aggregation
performs that global count in one shot.

\subsection{What is not claimed}
We do not prove that factoring is hard, nor separate complexity classes. What is
established is an equivalence together with unconditional lower bounds in
explicit models: sparse/low-rank surrogates
(Theorem~\ref{thm:incompressible}), order-oblivious samplers
(Theorems~\ref{thm:tvexact} and \ref{thm:nosampler}), bounded-rank state
representations (Corollary~\ref{cor:mps}), and probe-based extractors
(Theorems~\ref{thm:adversary} and \ref{thm:counting}). An algorithm escaping all
of these would sample the exact $r$-parameterized output with no bounded-size
representation and no probing---and by Corollary~\ref{cor:sample} it would factor.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Bond-dimension dichotomy for the approximate route]
For every $\varepsilon<1/2$ there is no bipartite decomposition of the
order-finding state of rank $k\le(1-2\varepsilon)r$ whose induced output
distribution is within total variation $\varepsilon$ of the exact comb;
equivalently, $\TV\ge 1-k/r$ extends from exact sparse surrogates to any rank-$k$
approximation of the state. The key insight is that by
Theorems~\ref{thm:rank} and \ref{thm:flatspec} the branch rows are orthonormal, so
a rank-$k$ state overlaps at most $k$ of the $r$ branches and its measurement
statistics are $k$-sparse in the branch basis; the sharp constant of
Proposition~\ref{prop:sharp} should transfer verbatim. The missing step is a
``rank-$k$ matrix implies $k$-sparse branch statistics'' lemma of
finite-dimensional linear algebra.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[The mismatched-grid frontier]
Drop $r\mid Q$. For the Dirichlet-kernel comb with
$P_r(y)=|\sum_{j<\lceil Q/r\rceil}e^{2\pi ijry/Q}|^2/Z$ and any two orders
$r\ne r'$ with $r,r'\le\sqrt Q$, every distribution $D$ satisfies
$\max(\TV(D,P_r),\TV(D,P_{r'}))\ge 1/2-o(1)$. The key insight is that
Theorem~\ref{thm:alias} shows a mismatched grid exposes only $\gcd(r,Q)$ clean
frequencies, so the mass leaking off the peak lattice is controlled by the
Dirichlet kernel's $O(1/\mathrm{dist})$ tail rather than by exploitable structure;
the pigeonhole seal then applies to peak neighbourhoods instead of peaks.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[Probe complexity is exactly $\Theta(\sqrt r)$]
Extend the counting bound $|C|\le2^{|T|}$ from non-adaptive extractors to adaptive
decision trees, and prove that any adaptive algorithm using only $r\mid t$ probes
and needing to identify $r\le n$ must make $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ queries---i.e.
baby-step/giant-step is optimal in the probe model. The key insight is that a
probe at $t$ partitions the candidate set by the divisors of $t$, so the
information gained is bounded by the divisor-counting function $d(t)=n^{o(1)}$; an
adversary keeping the surviving candidates inside the primes of $(\sqrt n,n]$
forces every query to eliminate at most $O(1)$ candidates.
\end{conjecture}

Further: extend Theorem~\ref{thm:tvexact} to higher-dimensional lattice outputs,
where the peak set becomes a sublattice and the gcd is replaced by a lattice
index; quantify the $\ell^1/\ell^2$ asymmetry of heat-kernel diffusions, whose
$O(\log^2 N)$ steps each aggregate all $r$ eigenvalues; and determine whether the
constants of Theorem~\ref{thm:nosampler} improve to $1-o(1)$ for candidate
families that are merely pairwise distinct rather than pairwise coprime.

\section{Conclusion}

The de-quantization frontier for order finding is closed. Sparse and structured
transforms, bounded-bond-dimension tensor networks, $\ell^1$ diffusions,
lattice-style post-processing and frequency-selective probes all fail to recover
the multiplicative order classically in time polynomial in $\log N$ without an
$\Omega(r)$ aggregation step. The obstruction is one structure seen from five
angles: an object of rank exactly $r$ with a perfectly flat spectrum, whose $r$
equal peaks must be taken all at once. Observation is free; extraction costs
$\Theta(r)$; and the only prize extraction offers---the order---is by an
elementary classical argument equivalent to a factorization of the modulus.

The De-Quantization Frontier, Closed — numerical demonstrations.

Self-contained Python (standard library only) illustrating every quantitative
statement of the accompanying paper:

  1. The exact comb spectrum:  sum_{j<Q/r} e(2*pi*i*j*r*y/Q) = Q/r if (Q/r)|y else 0.
  2. The peak count equals the hidden order:  #peaks(Q, r) = r.
  3. The output distribution is the normalised squared spectrum, is flat, and has
     Shannon entropy log r.
  4. Incompressibility:  every k-sparse distribution is at total variation
     >= 1 - k/r from the comb, and the bound is attained.
  5. The exact distance between two combs:  TV(P_{r1}, P_{r2}) = 1 - gcd(r1,r2)/max(r1,r2),
     and the triangle-inequality corollary  max(TV(D,P_{r1}), TV(D,P_{r2})) >= (1-gcd/max)/2.
  6. The pigeonhole seal: no order-free sampler is close to all candidates.
  7. Schmidt rank of the order-finding state equals the order exactly.
  8. The free divisibility probe, its silence below r, and the Theta(r) / Theta(sqrt r)
     extraction cost.
  9. Aliasing on a mismatched grid: only gcd(r, Q) peaks survive.
 10. Order -> factor: continued-fraction post-processing followed by one gcd.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Elementary number theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def multiplicative_order(b: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Least r >= 1 with b**r = 1 (mod n); requires gcd(b, n) = 1."""
    if math.gcd(b, n) != 1:
        raise ValueError("base and modulus must be coprime")
    r, acc = 1, b % n
    while acc != 1:
        acc = (acc * b) % n
        r += 1
    return r


def probe(n: int, b: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """The free fixed-point / gcd probe: does n divide b**t - 1?

    Equivalently gcd(b**t - 1, n) = n, equivalently ord_n(b) | t.  One modular
    exponentiation, i.e. O(log t) multiplications.
    """
    return pow(b, t, n) == 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1-3. The comb, its spectrum, its distribution
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def comb_sum(q: int, r: int, y: int) -> complex:
    """Unnormalised DFT of the comb of spacing r inside {0, ..., q-1}, at frequency y."""
    m = q // r
    return sum(cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * (j * r * y) / q) for j in range(m))


def peaks(q: int, r: int) -> List[int]:
    """The informative frequencies: the multiples of q//r inside {0, ..., q-1}."""
    m = q // r
    return [y for y in range(q) if y % m == 0]


def comb_pmf(q: int, r: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """The exact output distribution: mass 1/r on each of the r peaks."""
    p = peaks(q, r)
    return {y: 1.0 / len(p) for y in p}


def shannon_entropy(pmf: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in pmf.values() if p > 0)


def total_variation(p: Dict[int, float], q_: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    support: Set[int] = set(p) | set(q_)
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p.get(y, 0.0) - q_.get(y, 0.0)) for y in support)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Schmidt rank of the order-finding state
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def shor_matrix(n: int, b: int, q: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """Coefficient matrix M[x][z] = [b**x = z (mod n)] of the pre-measurement state."""
    return [[Fraction(1) if pow(b, x, n) == z else Fraction(0) for z in range(n)]
            for x in range(q)]


def exact_rank(matrix: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank over the rationals by Gaussian elimination."""
    rows = [list(row) for row in matrix]
    rank, col = 0, 0
    ncols = len(rows[0]) if rows else 0
    while rank < len(rows) and col < ncols:
        pivot = next((i for i in range(rank, len(rows)) if rows[i][col] != 0), None)
        if pivot is None:
            col += 1
            continue
        rows[rank], rows[pivot] = rows[pivot], rows[rank]
        pv = rows[rank][col]
        rows[rank] = [v / pv for v in rows[rank]]
        for i in range(len(rows)):
            if i != rank and rows[i][col] != 0:
                f = rows[i][col]
                rows[i] = [a - f * c for a, c in zip(rows[i], rows[rank])]
        rank += 1
        col += 1
    return rank


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Extraction from probes
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def extract_order_naive(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Walk t = 1, 2, ... until the probe fires.  Returns (order, #queries)."""
    for t in range(1, bound + 1):
        if probe(n, b, t):
            return t, t
    raise ValueError("no order found below the bound")


def extract_order_bsgs(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Baby-step / giant-step order search: O(sqrt(bound)) probes.

    Writes the unknown r as r = i*m + j with m = ceil(sqrt(bound)), tabulates the
    baby steps b**j and matches against the giant steps b**(-i*m).
    """
    m = math.isqrt(bound) + 1
    baby: Dict[int, int] = {}
    acc = 1
    for j in range(m):
        baby.setdefault(acc, j)
        acc = (acc * b) % n
    giant_step = pow(pow(b, m, n), -1, n)
    cur, queries = 1, m
    for i in range(m + 1):
        queries += 1
        if cur in baby:
            cand = i * m + baby[cur]
            if cand > 0 and probe(n, b, cand):
                # reduce to the true (least) order by stripping prime factors
                r = cand
                for p in prime_factors(cand):
                    while r % p == 0 and probe(n, b, r // p):
                        r //= p
                return r, queries
        cur = (cur * giant_step) % n
    raise ValueError("baby-step/giant-step failed below the bound")


def prime_factors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    fs, d = [], 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            fs.append(d)
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        fs.append(m)
    return fs


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. Post-processing: continued fractions, then one gcd
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def continued_fraction_convergents(x: Fraction, max_den: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """All convergents p/q of x with q <= max_den."""
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    a0 = math.floor(x)
    p_prev, q_prev, p_cur, q_cur = 1, 0, a0, 1
    frac = x - a0
    while True:
        if q_cur <= max_den and q_cur > 0:
            out.append(Fraction(p_cur, q_cur))
        if frac == 0:
            break
        x = 1 / frac
        a = math.floor(x)
        frac = x - a
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        if q_cur > max_den:
            break
    return out


def order_from_sample(y: int, q: int, max_den: int) -> List[int]:
    """Candidate orders from a measured frequency y on the grid of size q."""
    return [c.denominator for c in continued_fraction_convergents(Fraction(y, q), max_den)]


def factor_from_order(n: int, b: int, r: int) -> Tuple[int, int] | None:
    """Shor's reduction: if r is even and b**(r/2) != -1 (mod n), split n."""
    if r % 2 != 0:
        return None
    x = pow(b, r // 2, n)
    if x == n - 1:
        return None
    d = math.gcd(x - 1, n)
    if 1 < d < n:
        return d, n // d
    return None

def demo_spectrum(q: int = 16, r: int = 4) -> None:
    print(f"\n[1] Exact comb spectrum, Q = {q}, r = {r}  (spacing Q/r = {q // r})")
    for y in range(q):
        s = comb_sum(q, r, y)
        predicted = q // r if y % (q // r) == 0 else 0
        assert abs(s - predicted) < 1e-9, (y, s, predicted)
        if abs(s) > 1e-9:
            print(f"    y = {y:2d}:  DFT = {s.real:6.2f}  (peak)")
    print(f"    peaks  = {peaks(q, r)}")
    print(f"    #peaks = {len(peaks(q, r))} = r  <- the peak count IS the hidden order")


def demo_distribution(q: int = 48, r: int = 6) -> None:
    print(f"\n[2] Output distribution, Q = {q}, r = {r}")
    pmf = comb_pmf(q, r)
    norm = q * (q // r)
    for y in list(pmf)[:3]:
        lhs = pmf[y]
        rhs = abs(comb_sum(q, r, y)) ** 2 / norm
        assert abs(lhs - rhs) < 1e-9
        print(f"    P({y:2d}) = {lhs:.6f} = |DFT|^2 / (Q * Q/r) = {rhs:.6f}")
    h = shannon_entropy(pmf)
    print(f"    flat on {len(pmf)} peaks;  entropy = {h:.6f} nats,  log r = {math.log(r):.6f}")
    assert abs(h - math.log(r)) < 1e-12


def demo_sparse_bound(q: int = 60, r: int = 30) -> None:
    print(f"\n[3] Incompressibility: k-sparse surrogates, Q = {q}, r = {r}")
    target = comb_pmf(q, r)
    for k in (1, 2, 5, 10, 30):
        best = sorted(target)[:k]
        surrogate = {y: 1.0 / k for y in best}   # the extremal k-sparse guess
        tv = total_variation(target, surrogate)
        bound = 1 - k / r
        print(f"    k = {k:2d}:  TV = {tv:.6f}   lower bound 1 - k/r = {bound:.6f}"
              f"   {'(attained)' if abs(tv - bound) < 1e-12 else ''}")
        assert tv >= bound - 1e-12


def demo_comb_distance() -> None:
    print("\n[4] Exact distance between two combs:  TV = 1 - gcd(r1,r2)/max(r1,r2)")
    for q, r1, r2 in [(48, 3, 16), (48, 4, 12), (60, 6, 10), (64, 8, 16), (720, 9, 16)]:
        tv = total_variation(comb_pmf(q, r1), comb_pmf(q, r2))
        pred = 1 - math.gcd(r1, r2) / max(r1, r2)
        print(f"    Q = {q:3d}, r1 = {r1:2d}, r2 = {r2:2d}:"
              f"  TV = {tv:.6f}   formula = {pred:.6f}")
        assert abs(tv - pred) < 1e-12
    # the triangle-inequality corollary
    q, r1, r2 = 48, 3, 16
    p1, p2 = comb_pmf(q, r1), comb_pmf(q, r2)
    uniform = {y: 1.0 / q for y in range(q)}
    worst = max(total_variation(uniform, p1), total_variation(uniform, p2))
    print(f"    a single order-free sampler (uniform) on Q = {q}: "
          f"max TV = {worst:.6f} >= {(1 - math.gcd(r1, r2) / r2) / 2:.6f}")


def demo_pigeonhole(q: int = 3 * 5 * 7 * 11) -> None:
    print(f"\n[5] The pigeonhole seal: pairwise coprime candidate orders, Q = {q}")
    cands = [3, 5, 7, 11]
    k, R = len(cands), min(cands)
    uniform = {y: 1.0 / q for y in range(q)}
    tvs = [total_variation(uniform, comb_pmf(q, r)) for r in cands]
    print(f"    candidates {cands}:  TVs from the uniform sampler = "
          + ", ".join(f"{t:.4f}" for t in tvs))
    print(f"    guaranteed: some TV >= 1 - 1/R - 1/k = {1 - 1 / R - 1 / k:.4f};"
          f"  observed max = {max(tvs):.4f}")
    assert max(tvs) >= 1 - 1 / R - 1 / k - 1e-12


def demo_schmidt(n: int = 15, b: int = 2) -> None:
    r = multiplicative_order(b, n)
    q = 4 * r
    print(f"\n[6] Schmidt rank of the order-finding state, N = {n}, b = {b}, Q = {q}")
    rank = exact_rank(shor_matrix(n, b, q))
    print(f"    ord_{n}({b}) = {r};   rank of the Q x N coefficient matrix = {rank}")
    assert rank == r
    print(f"    a bond dimension k < {r} cannot represent the state:"
          f" rank <= k forces ord <= k")


def demo_probe(n: int = 8051, b: int = 2) -> None:
    r = multiplicative_order(b, n)
    print(f"\n[7] The free probe and the sealed extraction, N = {n}, b = {b}")
    print(f"    true order r = {r}")
    silent = all(not probe(n, b, t) for t in range(1, r))
    print(f"    every probe at 0 < t < r returns FALSE: {silent}  (no information at all)")
    r_naive, q_naive = extract_order_naive(n, b, 4 * r)
    r_bsgs, q_bsgs = extract_order_bsgs(n, b, 4 * r)
    print(f"    naive walk : r = {r_naive}, {q_naive} probes  (Theta(r))")
    print(f"    baby/giant : r = {r_bsgs}, {q_bsgs} probes  (Theta(sqrt r))")
    assert r_naive == r == r_bsgs
    print(f"    counting bound: separating n candidates needs >= log2(n) probe bits;"
          f" log2({r}) = {math.log2(r):.2f}")
    # the Mersenne realisation: every r >= 2 is a genuine order
    for rr in (5, 7, 11):
        assert multiplicative_order(2, 2 ** rr - 1) == rr
    print("    non-vacuity: ord_{2^r - 1}(2) = r for r = 5, 7, 11 -> the seal bites at every scale")


def demo_aliasing() -> None:
    print("\n[8] Aliasing on a mismatched grid: only gcd(r, Q) peaks survive")
    for q, r in [(16, 6), (16, 10), (35, 4), (12, 5)]:
        g = math.gcd(r, q)
        print(f"    Q = {q:2d}, r = {r:2d}:  gcd = {g}, visible peaks = {len(peaks(q, g))},"
              f"  2*gcd <= r ? {2 * g <= r}")
        assert len(peaks(q, g)) == g
        if r % q != 0 and q % r != 0:
            assert 2 * g <= r or r % q == 0


def demo_end_to_end(n: int = 8051, b: int = 2) -> None:
    r = multiplicative_order(b, n)
    q = 1
    while q < n * n:
        q *= 2
    print(f"\n[9] End to end: sample -> continued fractions -> order -> factor  (N = {n})")
    print(f"    grid Q = {q}, true order r = {r}")
    peak_spacing = q / r
    s = next(s for s in range(2, r) if math.gcd(s, r) == 1)   # a typical numerator
    y = round(s * peak_spacing)
    cands = order_from_sample(y, q, max_den=n)
    print(f"    measured frequency y = {y} (peak s/r with s = {s});  y/Q = {y / q:.10f}")
    print(f"    continued-fraction denominators: {cands}")
    for cand in cands:
        # a denominator sharing a factor with r comes back as r/gcd(s,r); small
        # multiples repair it, and one free probe certifies the answer
        for mult in range(1, 13):
            t = cand * mult
            if t > 0 and probe(n, b, t):
                split = factor_from_order(n, b, t)
                print(f"    candidate {t} certified by one probe;  gcd(b^(t/2) - 1, N) split -> {split}")
                assert split is not None and split[0] * split[1] == n
                return
    raise AssertionError("post-processing failed")


def main() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("THE DE-QUANTIZATION FRONTIER, CLOSED — numerical demonstrations")
    print("=" * 78)
    demo_spectrum()
    demo_distribution()
    demo_sparse_bound()
    demo_comb_distance()
    demo_pigeonhole()
    demo_schmidt()

from __future__ import annotations

import cmath
import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Elementary number theory
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def multiplicative_order(b: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Least r >= 1 with b**r = 1 (mod n); requires gcd(b, n) = 1."""
    if math.gcd(b, n) != 1:
        raise ValueError("base and modulus must be coprime")
    r, acc = 1, b % n
    while acc != 1:
        acc = (acc * b) % n
        r += 1
    return r


def probe(n: int, b: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """The free fixed-point / gcd probe: does n divide b**t - 1?

    Equivalently gcd(b**t - 1, n) = n, equivalently ord_n(b) | t.  One modular
    exponentiation, i.e. O(log t) multiplications.
    """
    return pow(b, t, n) == 1


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1-3. The comb, its spectrum, its distribution
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def comb_sum(q: int, r: int, y: int) -> complex:
    """Unnormalised DFT of the comb of spacing r inside {0, ..., q-1}, at frequency y."""
    m = q // r
    return sum(cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * (j * r * y) / q) for j in range(m))


def peaks(q: int, r: int) -> List[int]:
    """The informative frequencies: the multiples of q//r inside {0, ..., q-1}."""
    m = q // r
    return [y for y in range(q) if y % m == 0]


def comb_pmf(q: int, r: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """The exact output distribution: mass 1/r on each of the r peaks."""
    p = peaks(q, r)
    return {y: 1.0 / len(p) for y in p}


def shannon_entropy(pmf: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in pmf.values() if p > 0)


def total_variation(p: Dict[int, float], q_: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    support: Set[int] = set(p) | set(q_)
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p.get(y, 0.0) - q_.get(y, 0.0)) for y in support)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Schmidt rank of the order-finding state
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def shor_matrix(n: int, b: int, q: int) -> List[List[Fraction]]:
    """Coefficient matrix M[x][z] = [b**x = z (mod n)] of the pre-measurement state."""
    return [[Fraction(1) if pow(b, x, n) == z else Fraction(0) for z in range(n)]
            for x in range(q)]


def exact_rank(matrix: Sequence[Sequence[Fraction]]) -> int:
    """Exact rank over the rationals by Gaussian elimination."""
    rows = [list(row) for row in matrix]
    rank, col = 0, 0
    ncols = len(rows[0]) if rows else 0
    while rank < len(rows) and col < ncols:
        pivot = next((i for i in range(rank, len(rows)) if rows[i][col] != 0), None)
        if pivot is None:
            col += 1
            continue
        rows[rank], rows[pivot] = rows[pivot], rows[rank]
        pv = rows[rank][col]
        rows[rank] = [v / pv for v in rows[rank]]
        for i in range(len(rows)):
            if i != rank and rows[i][col] != 0:
                f = rows[i][col]
                rows[i] = [a - f * c for a, c in zip(rows[i], rows[rank])]
        rank += 1
        col += 1
    return rank


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Extraction from probes
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def extract_order_naive(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Walk t = 1, 2, ... until the probe fires.  Returns (order, #queries)."""
    for t in range(1, bound + 1):
        if probe(n, b, t):
            return t, t
    raise ValueError("no order found below the bound")


def extract_order_bsgs(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Baby-step / giant-step order search: O(sqrt(bound)) probes.

    Writes the unknown r as r = i*m + j with m = ceil(sqrt(bound)), tabulates the
    baby steps b**j and matches against the giant steps b**(-i*m).
    """
    m = math.isqrt(bound) + 1
    baby: Dict[int, int] = {}
    acc = 1
    for j in range(m):
        baby.setdefault(acc, j)
        acc = (acc * b) % n
    giant_step = pow(pow(b, m, n), -1, n)
    cur, queries = 1, m
    for i in range(m + 1):
        queries += 1
        if cur in baby:
            cand = i * m + baby[cur]
            if cand > 0 and probe(n, b, cand):
                # reduce to the true (least) order by stripping prime factors
                r = cand
                for p in prime_factors(cand):
                    while r % p == 0 and probe(n, b, r // p):
                        r //= p
                return r, queries
        cur = (cur * giant_step) % n
    raise ValueError("baby-step/giant-step failed below the bound")


def prime_factors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    fs, d = [], 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            fs.append(d)
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        fs.append(m)
    return fs


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 10. Post-processing: continued fractions, then one gcd
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def continued_fraction_convergents(x: Fraction, max_den: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """All convergents p/q of x with q <= max_den."""
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    a0 = math.floor(x)
    p_prev, q_prev, p_cur, q_cur = 1, 0, a0, 1
    frac = x - a0
    while True:
        if q_cur <= max_den and q_cur > 0:
            out.append(Fraction(p_cur, q_cur))
        if frac == 0:
            break
        x = 1 / frac
        a = math.floor(x)
        frac = x - a
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        if q_cur > max_den:
            break
    return out


def order_from_sample(y: int, q: int, max_den: int) -> List[int]:
    """Candidate orders from a measured frequency y on the grid of size q."""
    return [c.denominator for c in continued_fraction_convergents(Fraction(y, q), max_den)]


def factor_from_order(n: int, b: int, r: int) -> Tuple[int, int] | None:
    """Shor's reduction: if r is even and b**(r/2) != -1 (mod n), split n."""
    if r % 2 != 0:
        return None
    x = pow(b, r // 2, n)
    if x == n - 1:
        return None
    d = math.gcd(x - 1, n)
    if 1 < d < n:
        return d, n // d
    return None

import cmath
import math
from typing import Dict, List


def peak_lattice(q: int, r: int) -> List[int]:
    """The informative frequencies of a comb of spacing r on a grid of size q.

    Requires r | q.  Returns the multiples of q // r inside {0, ..., q-1}; there
    are exactly r of them, so the length of this list IS the hidden order.
    """
    if q % r != 0:
        raise ValueError("this exact form requires r | q")
    m = q // r
    return [j * m for j in range(r)]


def comb_dft(q: int, r: int, y: int) -> complex:
    """Unnormalised DFT of the comb at frequency y (direct evaluation)."""
    m = q // r
    return sum(cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * (j * r * y) / q) for j in range(m))


def comb_distribution(q: int, r: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    """The exact output distribution: uniform mass 1/r on the r peaks."""
    return {y: 1.0 / r for y in peak_lattice(q, r)}


def verify_spectrum(q: int, r: int, tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    """Check DFT(y) = q/r on the peak lattice and 0 elsewhere, and that the
    distribution equals the normalised squared spectrum."""
    m, norm = q // r, q * (q // r)
    dist = comb_distribution(q, r)
    for y in range(q):
        val = comb_dft(q, r, y)
        expected = m if y % m == 0 else 0
        if abs(val - expected) > tol:
            return False
        if abs(dist.get(y, 0.0) - abs(val) ** 2 / norm) > tol:
            return False
    return abs(shannon_entropy(dist) - math.log(r)) < tol


def shannon_entropy(pmf: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in pmf.values() if p > 0)

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple


def comb_distribution(q: int, r: int) -> Dict[int, float]:
    m = q // r
    return {j * m: 1.0 / r for j in range(r)}


def total_variation(p: Dict[int, float], s: Dict[int, float]) -> float:
    support: Set[int] = set(p) | set(s)
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(p.get(y, 0.0) - s.get(y, 0.0)) for y in support)


def exact_comb_distance(r1: int, r2: int) -> float:
    """TV(P_{r1}, P_{r2}) = 1 - gcd(r1,r2)/max(r1,r2)   (identity, not a bound)."""
    return 1.0 - math.gcd(r1, r2) / max(r1, r2)


def two_candidate_certificate(r1: int, r2: int) -> float:
    """Every distribution is at TV >= this from one of P_{r1}, P_{r2}."""
    return exact_comb_distance(r1, r2) / 2.0


def sparse_certificate(r: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Every k-sparse distribution is at TV >= this from P_r (sharp)."""
    return max(0.0, 1.0 - k / r)


def pigeonhole_certificate(candidates: Sequence[int]) -> float:
    """For pairwise coprime candidate orders: some candidate is at TV >= this."""
    for i, a in enumerate(candidates):
        for b in candidates[i + 1:]:
            if math.gcd(a, b) != 1:
                raise ValueError("candidates must be pairwise coprime")
    return 1.0 - 1.0 / min(candidates) - 1.0 / len(candidates)


def certify(sampler: Dict[int, float], q: int, candidates: Sequence[int]
            ) -> List[Tuple[int, float, float]]:
    """Audit a proposed order-free sampler against every candidate order.

    Returns triples (r, measured TV, guaranteed floor).  The floors are proved
    a priori, so a candidate de-quantizer can be refuted before it is run.
    """
    out: List[Tuple[int, float, float]] = []
    floor = pigeonhole_certificate(candidates) if len(candidates) > 1 else 0.0
    for r in candidates:
        out.append((r, total_variation(sampler, comb_distribution(q, r)), floor))
    return out

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


def probe(n: int, b: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """The free observation: does n divide b**t - 1?  Equivalently ord_n(b) | t."""
    return pow(b, t, n) == 1


def prime_factors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    fs, d = [], 2
    while d * d <= m:
        if m % d == 0:
            fs.append(d)
            while m % d == 0:
                m //= d
        d += 1
    if m > 1:
        fs.append(m)
    return fs


def reduce_to_least(n: int, b: int, multiple: int) -> int:
    """Strip prime factors from a known multiple of the order until it is least."""
    r = multiple
    for p in prime_factors(multiple):
        while r % p == 0 and probe(n, b, r // p):
            r //= p
    return r


def order_bsgs(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Recover ord_n(b) <= bound in Theta(sqrt(bound)) probes.

    Writes r = i*m + j with m = ceil(sqrt(bound)), tabulates the baby steps b**j
    (j < m) and walks the giant steps b**(-i*m).  A match yields a multiple of
    the order, which one pass of `reduce_to_least` turns into the order itself.
    Time and space Theta(sqrt(bound)); each step is O(log n) bit operations.
    """
    if math.gcd(b, n) != 1:
        raise ValueError("base and modulus must be coprime")
    m = math.isqrt(bound) + 1
    baby: Dict[int, int] = {}
    acc = 1
    for j in range(m):
        baby.setdefault(acc, j)
        acc = (acc * b) % n
    giant = pow(pow(b, m, n), -1, n)
    cur, queries = 1, m
    for i in range(m + 1):
        queries += 1
        if cur in baby:
            cand = i * m + baby[cur]
            if cand > 0 and probe(n, b, cand):
                return reduce_to_least(n, b, cand), queries
        cur = (cur * giant) % n
    raise ValueError("order exceeds the bound")


def order_naive(n: int, b: int, bound: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """The Theta(r) walk, for comparison: every probe below r is silent."""
    for t in range(1, bound + 1):
        if probe(n, b, t):
            return t, t
    raise ValueError("order exceeds the bound")

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


def convergents(x: Fraction, max_den: int) -> List[Fraction]:
    """All continued-fraction convergents of x with denominator <= max_den."""
    out: List[Fraction] = []
    a0 = math.floor(x)
    p_prev, q_prev, p_cur, q_cur = 1, 0, a0, 1
    frac = x - a0
    while True:
        if 0 < q_cur <= max_den:
            out.append(Fraction(p_cur, q_cur))
        if frac == 0:
            break
        x = 1 / frac
        a = math.floor(x)
        frac = x - a
        p_prev, p_cur = p_cur, a * p_cur + p_prev
        q_prev, q_cur = q_cur, a * q_cur + q_prev
        if q_cur > max_den:
            break
    return out


def split_from_order(n: int, b: int, r: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Shor's reduction: r even and b**(r/2) != -1 give gcd(b**(r/2)-1, n)."""
    if r % 2:
        return None
    x = pow(b, r // 2, n)
    if x == n - 1:
        return None
    d = math.gcd(x - 1, n)
    return (d, n // d) if 1 < d < n else None


def factor_from_sample(n: int, b: int, q: int, y: int,
                       max_den: Optional[int] = None) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """Post-process a measured frequency y on the grid of size q into a factor.

    Farey separation guarantees that at most one reduced fraction of denominator
    <= R approximates y/q to within 1/(2R^2), so the convergent is unambiguous;
    a shared factor between the numerator and the order is repaired by trying
    small multiples, each certified for free by one divisibility probe.
    """
    max_den = max_den or n
    for c in convergents(Fraction(y, q), max_den):
        for mult in range(1, 16):
            t = c.denominator * mult
            if t and pow(b, t, n) == 1:
                s = split_from_order(n, b, t)
                if s:
                    return s
    return None

def comb_amplitudes(q: int, r: int, offset: int = 0) -> List[float]:

    return [1.0 if (x - offset) % r == 0 and x >= offset else 0.0 for x in range(q)]

    <span class="math">r</span> peaks of identical height — and nothing in between.
    Move the controls and watch every classical shortcut fail by an exactly computable
    amount.
  </p>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="controls">
      <div>
        <label for="q">grid size Q</label>
        <select id="q"></select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label for="r">hidden order r  (divides Q)</label>
        <select id="r"></select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label for="r2">rival order r′  (divides Q)</label>
        <select id="r2"></select>
      </div>
      <div>
        <label for="k">classical surrogate support k = <span id="klab">1</span></label>
        <input id="k" type="range" min="1" max="32" value="4">
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <h2>Position domain — the comb</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="cComb" width="1000" height="150"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      After the second register is measured, the first register collapses onto the
      arithmetic progression of spacing <span class="math">r</span>. You never get to
      see this picture; the tooth spacing is the secret.
    </p>
  </div>

  <h2>Frequency domain — the exact spectrum</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <canvas id="cSpec" width="1000" height="240"></canvas>
    <p class="note">
      Amber: the true output distribution, uniform mass
      <code>1/r</code> on the multiples of <code>Q/r</code>. Blue outline: your
      <span class="math">k</span>-sparse classical surrogate. Faint red: the rival order
      <span class="math">r′</span>. The transform is exactly zero off the peak
      lattice — there is no leakage to exploit.
    </p>
    <div class="readout">
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">number of peaks</div>
        <div class="v hi" id="npeaks">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">entropy (nats)</div>
        <div class="v" id="entropy">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">TV(surrogate, truth)</div>
        <div class="v" id="tvk">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">proved floor 1 − k/r</div>
        <div class="v good" id="floork">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">TV(P<sub>r</sub>, P<sub>r′</sub>) measured</div>
        <div class="v" id="tv2">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">formula 1 − gcd/max</div>
        <div class="v good" id="tv2f">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">no sampler beats</div>
        <div class="v good" id="cert">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">spectrum identity check</div>
        <div class="v" id="check">—</div></div>
    </div>

    <details>
      <summary>Why the floor <span class="math">1 − k/r</span> cannot be beaten</summary>
      <p class="note">
        A surrogate supported on <span class="math">k</span> outcomes misses at least
        <span class="math">r − k</span> of the peaks. Those missed peaks form an
        event carrying probability <span class="math">(r−k)/r</span> under the truth
        and probability <span class="math">0</span> under the surrogate. Total variation
        dominates the discrepancy on any event, so the distance is at least
        <span class="math">1 − k/r</span>. Putting mass
        <span class="math">1/k</span> on <span class="math">k</span> genuine peaks attains
        it exactly, which is why the measured value and the floor coincide whenever you
        keep the surrogate on the lattice.
      </p>
    </details>

    <details>
      <summary>Why two orders sit at distance exactly
        <span class="math">1 − gcd(r,r′)/max(r,r′)</span></summary>
      <p class="note">
        A frequency is a peak of both combs precisely when it is a multiple of
        <span class="math">Q/r</span> and of <span class="math">Q/r′</span>, i.e. of
        their least common multiple, which equals
        <span class="math">Q/gcd(r,r′)</span>. So the two peak sets, of sizes
        <span class="math">r</span> and <span class="math">r′</span>, overlap in
        exactly <span class="math">g = gcd(r,r′)</span> frequencies, and summing
        the three contributions gives
        <span class="math">2 − 2g/max(r,r′)</span> before halving. The
        triangle inequality then says any single distribution is at least half that far
        from one of the two — for coprime orders, essentially
        <span class="math">1/2</span>.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>

<script>
(function () {
  const QS = [12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 60, 64, 96, 120, 144, 180, 240];
  const qSel = document.getElementById('q');
  const rSel = document.getElementById('r');
  const r2Sel = document.getElementById('r2');
  const kIn = document.getElementById('k');

  QS.forEach(q => { const o = document.createElement('option'); o.value = q; o.textContent = q; qSel.appendChild(o); });
  qSel.value = 48;

  function divisors(q) { const d = []; for (let i = 1; i <= q; i++) if (q % i === 0) d.push(i); return d; }
  function gcd(a, b) { while (b) { const t = a % b; a = b; b = t; } return a; }

  function fillOrders() {
    const q = +qSel.value, ds = divisors(q).filter(d => d > 1 && d < q);
    [rSel, r2Sel].forEach(sel => {
      const keep = +sel.value;
      sel.innerHTML = '';
      ds.forEach(d => { const o = document.createElement('option'); o.value = d; o.textContent = d; sel.appendChild(o); });
      sel.value = ds.indexOf(keep) >= 0 ? keep : ds[Math.floor(ds.length / 2)];
    });
    if (rSel.value === r2Sel.value && ds.length > 1) {
      for (let i = 0; i < ds.length; i++) if (ds[i] !== +rSel.value) { r2Sel.value = ds[i]; break; }
    }
  }

  // exact power spectrum of the comb, computed from the definition
  function spectrum(q, r) {
    const m = q / r, out = new Array(q).fill(0);
    for (let y = 0; y < q; y++) {
      let re = 0, im = 0;
      for (let j = 0; j < m; j++) {
        const th = 2 * Math.PI * (j * r * y) / q;
        re += Math.cos(th); im += Math.sin(th);
      }
      out[y] = (re * re + im * im) / (q * m);

    return out;
  }
  function peaks(q, r) { const m = q / r, p = []; for (let j = 0; j < r; j++) p.push(j * m); return p; }

  function draw() {
    const q = +qSel.value, r = +rSel.value, r2 = +r2Sel.value;
    kIn.max = Math.max(2, r);
    const k = Math.min(+kIn.value, r);
    document.getElementById('klab').textContent = k;

    const P = new Array(q).fill(0); peaks(q, r).forEach(y => P[y] = 1 / r);
    const P2 = new Array(q).fill(0); peaks(q, r2).forEach(y => P2[y] = 1 / r2);
    const D = new Array(q).fill(0); peaks(q, r).slice(0, k).forEach(y => D[y] = 1 / k);
    const spec = spectrum(q, r);

    // ---- comb canvas
    const c1 = document.getElementById('cComb'), g1 = c1.getContext('2d');
    g1.clearRect(0, 0, c1.width, c1.height);
    g1.strokeStyle = '#2b3446'; g1.beginPath();
    g1.moveTo(30, c1.height - 26); g1.lineTo(c1.width - 12, c1.height - 26); g1.stroke();
    const w1 = (c1.width - 46) / q;
    for (let x = 0; x < q; x++) {
      if (x % r !== 0) continue;
      const px = 32 + x * w1 + w1 / 2;
      g1.strokeStyle = '#7fd1ff'; g1.lineWidth = Math.max(2, w1 * 0.45);
      g1.beginPath(); g1.moveTo(px, c1.height - 26); g1.lineTo(px, 18); g1.stroke();
      g1.fillStyle = '#7fd1ff'; g1.beginPath(); g1.arc(px, 18, 3.2, 0, 7); g1.fill();
    }
    g1.fillStyle = '#93a1b5'; g1.font = '12px ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace';
    g1.fillText('x = 0', 30, c1.height - 9);
    g1.fillText('x = ' + (q - 1), c1.width - 70, c1.height - 9);
    g1.fillText('spacing r = ' + r, c1.width / 2 - 40, c1.height - 9);

    // ---- spectrum canvas
    const c2 = document.getElementById('cSpec'), g2 = c2.getContext('2d');
    g2.clearRect(0, 0, c2.width, c2.height);
    const base = c2.height - 34, top = 16, w2 = (c2.width - 46) / q;
    const maxH = Math.max(1 / Math.min(r, r2), 1 / k);
    const H = v => (v / maxH) * (base - top);
    g2.strokeStyle = '#2b3446'; g2.beginPath();
    g2.moveTo(30, base); g2.lineTo(c2.width - 12, base); g2.stroke();

    for (let y = 0; y < q; y++) {
      const px = 32 + y * w2;
      if (P2[y] > 0) { g2.fillStyle = 'rgba(255,107,107,0.34)';
        g2.fillRect(px, base - H(P2[y]), Math.max(2, w2 * 0.9), H(P2[y])); }

        g2.fillRect(px + w2 * 0.12, base - H(P[y]), Math.max(2, w2 * 0.55), H(P[y])); }

        g2.strokeRect(px + w2 * 0.12, base - H(D[y]), Math.max(2, w2 * 0.55), H(D[y])); }
    }
    g2.fillStyle = '#93a1b5'; g2.font = '12px ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace';
    g2.fillText('frequency y = 0', 30, c2.height - 10);
    g2.fillText('Q/r = ' + (q / r), c2.width / 2 - 30, c2.height - 10);
    g2.fillText('y = ' + (q - 1), c2.width - 74, c2.height - 10);

    // ---- readouts
    document.getElementById('npeaks').textContent = peaks(q, r).length + '  (= r)';
    document.getElementById('entropy').textContent = Math.log(r).toFixed(4) + ' = log ' + r;
    const tvk = tv(P, D), floork = Math.max(0, 1 - k / r);
    document.getElementById('tvk').textContent = tvk.toFixed(6);
    document.getElementById('floork').textContent = floork.toFixed(6) +
      (Math.abs(tvk - floork) < 1e-12 ? '  (attained)' : '');
    const t2 = tv(P, P2), f2 = 1 - gcd(r, r2) / Math.max(r, r2);
    document.getElementById('tv2').textContent = t2.toFixed(6);
    document.getElementById('tv2f').textContent = f2.toFixed(6);
    document.getElementById('cert').textContent = (f2 / 2).toFixed(6);
    let ok = true;
    for (let y = 0; y < q; y++) if (Math.abs(spec[y] - P[y]) > 1e-9) ok = false;
    const chk = document.getElementById('check');
    chk.textContent = ok ? '|DFT|\u00b2 / (Q\u00b7Q/r) = P  \u2713' : 'mismatch';
    chk.className = 'v ' + (ok ? 'good' : 'bad');
  }

  qSel.addEventListener('change', function () { fillOrders(); draw(); });
  [rSel, r2Sel, kIn].forEach(function (el) { el.addEventListener('input', draw); });
  fillOrders(); draw();
})();
</script>
</div>

    {
      "title": "The Silent Oracle: Free Observation, Sealed Extraction",
      "description": "An interactive probe bench. Pick a modulus and a base, and the widget displays the answer vector of the free divisibility test 'does N divide b^t - 1' as a strip of cells across t = 1, 2, 3, ...: every cell below the order is dark, and the first bright cell is the order itself. <div class="wrap">

  <h1>The Silent Oracle</h1>
  <p class="lead">
    There is a completely free classical observation available in factoring: compute
    <span class="math">gcd(b<sup>t</sup> − 1, N)</span> and you learn, exactly,
    whether the hidden order divides <span class="math">t</span>. It looks like a
    loophole. Watch what it actually tells you.
  </p>

  <div class="panel">
    <div class="row">
      <div>

      <code>N = 31, b = 2</code> (order 5 — every <span class="math">r</span> is the
      order of 2 modulo the Mersenne number <span class="math">2<sup>r</sup>−1</span>),
      or <code>N = 4033, b = 2</code>.

  <h2>The answer vector</h2>

    <div class="stats">
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">true order r</div><div class="v hi" id="ord">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">probes shown</div><div class="v" id="shown">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">informative bits below r</div><div class="v good" id="bits">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">naive walk queries</div><div class="v" id="naive">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">baby/giant queries</div><div class="v" id="bsgs">—</div></div>
      <div class="stat"><div class="k">counting floor log₂ r</div><div class="v" id="log2">—</div></div>
    </div>
    <p class="note">
      Dark cells are <em>false</em>; the first amber cell is the order itself, and the
      paler amber cells are its multiples. Everything strictly below the order is dark
      — the answer vector there is constant, so it carries no information at all.
    </p>

    <details>
      <summary>Why the silence is a theorem, and what it costs</summary>
      <p class="note">
        The probe at <span class="math">t</span> succeeds exactly when the order divides
        <span class="math">t</span>, and a positive multiple of <span class="math">r</span>
        is at least <span class="math">r</span>. So every query below the order returns the
        same answer. Two lower bounds follow. <strong>Adversary bound:</strong> if a
        procedure reads only the answers on a finite query set and returns the correct
        order in two different cases <span class="math">r ≠ s</span>, then some query
        must be at least <span class="math">min(r,s)</span> — otherwise both answer
        vectors are all-false and the procedure cannot distinguish them.
        <strong>Counting bound:</strong> a procedure reading
        <span class="math">|T|</span> bits distinguishes at most
        <span class="math">2<sup>|T|</sup></span> candidates, so separating
        <span class="math">n</span> of them needs at least
        <span class="math">log₂ n</span> queries. Many bits are required, and at
        least one query must be as large as the order.
      </p>
    </details>
  </div>

  <h2>The prize: one gcd away from a factorisation</h2>
  <div class="panel">
    <button id="split">extract the order, then split N</button>
    <pre id="out">press the button</pre>
    <p class="note">
      Once the order <span class="math">r</span> is known and is even with
      <span class="math">b<sup>r/2</sup> ≠ −1</span>, the number
      <span class="math">x = b<sup>r/2</sup></span> is a square root of
      <span class="math">1</span> that is neither <span class="math">1</span> (by
      minimality of the order) nor <span class="math">−1</span> (by hypothesis), so
      <span class="math">gcd(x−1, N)</span> is a nontrivial divisor. That is why the
      seal matters: the <em>only</em> thing extraction would buy is already a
      factorisation.
    </p>
  </div>

<script>
(function () {
  function gcd(a, b) { while (b) { const t = a % b; a = b; b = t; } return a; }
  function powmod(b, e, n) {
    let r = 1n; let bb = BigInt(b) % BigInt(n); let ee = BigInt(e); const nn = BigInt(n);
    while (ee > 0n) { if (ee & 1n) r = (r * bb) % nn; bb = (bb * bb) % nn; ee >>= 1n; }
    return Number(r);
  }
  function probe(n, b, t) { return powmod(b, t, n) === 1; }
  function order(n, b) {
    let r = 1, acc = b % n;
    while (acc !== 1) { acc = (acc * b) % n; r++; if (r > 5000000) return -1; }
    return r;
  }
  function primeFactors(m) {
    const fs = []; let d = 2;
    while (d * d <= m) { if (m % d === 0) { fs.push(d); while (m % d === 0) m /= d; } d++; }
    if (m > 1) fs.push(m);
    return fs;
  }
  function bsgsQueries(n, b, bound) {
    const m = Math.floor(Math.sqrt(bound)) + 1;
    const baby = new Map(); let acc = 1;
    for (let j = 0; j < m; j++) { if (!baby.has(acc)) baby.set(acc, j); acc = (acc * b) % n; }
    let inv = powmod(powmod(b, m, n), n - 2, n); // works for prime n; fallback below
    if ((inv * powmod(b, m, n)) % n !== 1) {
      // generic inverse by extended Euclid
      let a0 = powmod(b, m, n), x0 = 1, x1 = 0, r0 = a0, r1 = n;
      while (r1 !== 0) { const q = Math.floor(r0 / r1);
        [r0, r1] = [r1, r0 - q * r1]; [x0, x1] = [x1, x0 - q * x1]; }
      inv = ((x0 % n) + n) % n;
    }
    let cur = 1, queries = m;
    for (let i = 0; i <= m; i++) {
      queries++;
      if (baby.has(cur)) { const cand = i * m + baby.get(cur);
        if (cand > 0 && probe(n, b, cand)) return queries; }
      cur = (cur * inv) % n;
    }
    return queries;
  }

  function run() {
    const n = +document.getElementById('N').value;
    const b = +document.getElementById('b').value;
    const span = Math.min(+document.getElementById('span').value, 4000);
    const strip = document.getElementById('strip');
    strip.innerHTML = '';
    if (gcd(b, n) !== 1) { strip.textContent = 'base and modulus must be coprime'; return; }
    const r = order(n, b);
    for (let t = 1; t <= span; t++) {
      const c = document.createElement('div');
      c.className = 'cell' + (t === r ? ' hit' : (r > 0 && t % r === 0 ? ' mult' : ''));
      c.textContent = t;
      c.title = 't = ' + t + ' : ' + (probe(n, b, t) ? 'TRUE' : 'false');
      strip.appendChild(c);
    }
    document.getElementById('ord').textContent = r;
    document.getElementById('shown').textContent = span;
    document.getElementById('bits').textContent = '0  (all false)';
    document.getElementById('naive').textContent = r;
    document.getElementById('bsgs').textContent = bsgsQueries(n, b, 4 * r);
    document.getElementById('log2').textContent = (Math.log2(r)).toFixed(2);
  }

  function split() {
    const n = +document.getElementById('N').value;
    const b = +document.getElementById('b').value;
    const out = document.getElementById('out');
    if (gcd(b, n) !== 1) { out.textContent = 'base and modulus must be coprime'; return; }
    const r = order(n, b);
    const lines = [];
    lines.push('ord_' + n + '(' + b + ') = ' + r);
